name: Scattering of particles

origin.note: Scattering in SILBOT first appeared at AINA 2023 (Navarra, Prencipe, Bonini, Tracolli, "Scattering with programmable matter", pp. 236–247), as the journal version states; that paper was not read and its DOI was not verified, so the journal version (Navarra, Piselli, Prencipe) is cited.

related.relation: Robots in the plane scatter to distinct points; particles must scatter so that no two are neighbours.

summary: Particles must reach a configuration in which no two particles occupy neighbouring nodes.
statement: From any initial **configuration** of $n$ **contracted** particles (each occupying one node of the triangular lattice), the particles must reach a configuration in which no two occupy neighbouring nodes (a **scattered** configuration), and stop.

primer.intro: Picture people standing in a crowded square who must spread out until nobody is standing right next to anyone else. The floor is the **triangular lattice**: the endless graph whose **nodes** are the corners of a tiling of the plane by equal triangles; each node is joined by an edge to six others, its **neighbours**. A **particle** occupies one node and moves in two actions: an **expansion** into an empty neighbouring node, after which it occupies both, then a **contraction** into one of the two; so one expansion and one contraction move it by one node. There are $n$ particles, each occupying one node at the start; the set of occupied nodes is the **configuration**. The particles are **oblivious** (they remember nothing from one action to the next) and **silent** (they send no messages); each decides only from what it sees around it. The goal is to reach a **scattered** configuration, where no two particles occupy neighbouring nodes, and then stop moving. The basic question is whether this is possible at all, from every starting configuration.

ideas.title: Activated only when crowded
ideas.idea:
Navarra, Piselli and Prencipe [Navarra2025Scattering] let each particle see only its six neighbouring nodes, give the particles no common sense of direction, and use **event-driven activation**: a contracted particle is activated (it gets a turn to act, an **activation**) as soon as it has a neighbour, and only then.

1. A particle with no neighbour is never activated, so it stays put.
2. An activated particle looks around itself and finds the longest run $I$ of consecutive empty neighbouring nodes.
3. If $I$ has 3, 4 or 5 nodes, the particle makes an expansion into the most central node of $I$ (in a tie, the one it sees as rightmost), and a contraction into that node once it is free; otherwise it stays.
4. When no particle has a neighbour, no particle is activated again: the task is done and the particles have stopped.
ideas.analysis: Event-driven activation gives stopping for free: a scattered configuration is exactly one in which nobody is ever activated again. The difficulty is choosing the local rule so that crowded particles really do spread out instead of moving back and forth forever. The proof looks at the smallest regular hexagon around a fixed centre that contains all particles: a particle on its border never moves inwards, each particle moves away from the centre at most $n-1$ times (Lemma 4 of [Navarra2025Scattering]), so the particles on the outermost hexagon end with no neighbour, and induction on $n$ handles the rest (Theorem 6). The paper gives no bound on rounds or moves.
ideas.why_it_matters: It shows how much the choice of scheduler can replace memory: with a 1-hop view and the usual asynchronous scheduler scattering is impossible (Theorem 4 of [Navarra2025Scattering]), but with event-driven activation particles without memory scatter and stop.

ideas.title: A crowded hexagon must spread over three times its area
ideas.idea: This simple counting argument is ours; the catalogue records no lower bound on time or moves. In the triangular lattice every small triangle of three mutually neighbouring nodes can hold at most one particle of a scattered configuration. Counting triangles, a region with $N$ nodes can hold at most about $N/3$ scattered particles. Now start with the $n$ particles packed into a full hexagon of radius $r$ (it has about $3r^2 = n$ nodes). The hexagon of radius $1.5r$ around the same centre has about $6.75r^2$ nodes, so it can hold only about $2.25r^2 = 0.75n$ scattered particles.
ideas.analysis: So about $n/4$ particles must end more than $1.5r$ from the centre, having started within $r$ of it: each travels at least $r/2$, which is about $\sqrt n$ nodes. That is at least about $n\sqrt n$ moves in total, and, if the scheduler lets each particle act once per **round** (an interval of time in which every particle is activated at least once), about $\sqrt n$ rounds. [Navarra2025Scattering] give no bound on rounds or moves, so how close their algorithm comes to these numbers is unknown.
ideas.why_it_matters: It shows that scattering, unlike gathering, forces the occupied region to grow in area, which costs real movement.

glossary.definition: an anonymous computing unit of constant size that occupies one node of the triangular lattice, or two neighbouring nodes while it moves
the infinite graph $G_\Delta$ whose nodes are the corners of a tiling of the plane by equilateral triangles; every node has six neighbours
a point of the triangular lattice; it is empty or occupied by a particle (an expanded particle occupies two)
two nodes are neighbours when an edge of the triangular lattice joins them; two particles are neighbours when they occupy neighbouring nodes
the action in which a particle that occupies one node extends into an empty neighbouring node and then occupies both
the action in which a particle that occupies two nodes withdraws into one of them
the set of nodes occupied by the particles
a configuration is scattered when no two particles occupy neighbouring nodes
keeping no state between activations: a particle decides from its current view only
sending no messages: a particle learns only which of its neighbouring nodes are occupied
one action of a particle chosen by the scheduler: it looks at its neighbourhood, updates its state and performs at most one expansion or contraction
a scheduler under which a particle is activated as soon as it has a neighbour, and only then
an interval of time in which every particle is activated at least once (an asynchronous round); a bound holds for every division of the execution into consecutive rounds

history: Scattering was posed for **silent, oblivious** particles, where the question is solvability without memory or messages. Navarra, Piselli and Prencipe restrict the 2-hop view of SILBOT to 1 hop; then scattering is unsolvable under the asynchronous scheduler, solvable without obstacles when a particle is activated as soon as it has a neighbour, and unsolvable with obstacles even under a synchronous scheduler [Navarra2025Scattering].

variants.title: SILBOT
variants.summary: With a 1-hop view and adversarial activation, silent oblivious particles cannot scatter; with the 2-hop view of SILBOT the question is open.

preconditions: Theorem 4: deterministic, 1-hop view, no common direction and no chirality
a particle with no neighbour must never move
three particles in a row: whatever a particle with one neighbour does, a fair asynchronous adversary makes the middle particle move back and forth forever
open with the 2-hop view of SILBOT

time.note: Impossible with a 1-hop view (Theorem 4); open with the 2-hop view of SILBOT. Event-driven activation makes it solvable.

open: Is scattering solvable in SILBOT with its original 2-hop view under adversarial activation? [Navarra2025Scattering] leave it open.
variants.notes: Model of [Navarra2025Scattering] (Section 2): SILBOT particles are silent, oblivious and disoriented, all operations are non-atomic, and a fair adversary decides activations; for scattering the view is restricted to 1 hop. The impossibility uses three particles in a row (Figures 3 and 4): a particle with one neighbour must move, either straight away from it or to one of two symmetric nodes, and in both cases the adversary makes the middle particle move back and forth forever. Theorem 7 (obstacles, even synchronous) is recorded on the event-driven setting. Checked against the full text.

variants.title: SILBOT with event-driven activation
variants.summary: Under event-driven activation, silent oblivious particles with a 1-hop view and no common direction scatter from any configuration without obstacles.

results.note: Introductory and current best (Theorem 6, Corollary 2): the rule of the primer, from any configuration of contracted particles, connected or not; particles share no direction and no chirality. No bound on rounds or moves.

time.note: Finite; no round bound and no lower bound.

moves.note: No move bound is given; each particle moves away from the centre of the enclosing hexagon at most $n-1$ times (Lemma 4).

open: Bound the rounds and moves of scattering under event-driven activation [Navarra2025Scattering].

Scattering with obstacles: unsolvable deterministically with a 1-hop view even under a synchronous scheduler (Theorem 7 of [Navarra2025Scattering]); which extra capability (chirality, a 2-hop view, randomised choices) makes it solvable?
variants.notes: Scattering is Simple Distancing (Definition 4 of [Navarra2025Scattering]): eventually every particle is contracted and has no neighbour; under event-driven activation the particles then stop. The proof takes the smallest regular hexagon around a fixed centre containing all particles: no particle on its border moves inwards (Lemma 3), each particle moves outwards at most $n-1$ times (Lemma 4), and induction on $n$ finishes (Theorem 6). With obstacles, where Strong Distancing also asks particles to keep away from obstacles, the problem is unsolvable even under a synchronous scheduler, in which only particles with a neighbour may move (Theorem 7); the paper then tests heuristic rules with randomised tie-breaking in simulation only. Checked against the full text.

figure.caption: Scattering under event-driven activation [Navarra2025Scattering]: from a configuration of contracted particles, here a triangle of ten, the particles must reach a configuration in which no two occupy neighbouring nodes, and stop. A particle is activated only while it has a neighbour (blue). An activated particle finds its longest run of consecutive empty neighbouring nodes; if the run has 3, 4 or 5 nodes, it makes an expansion into the middle node (outlined: the activated particles that move) and then a contraction there, otherwise it stays. In this run every activated particle acts in each step and all particles break ties the same way; isolated particles (green) are never activated again.

frames.label: Start: a crowded triangle; every particle with a neighbour is activated
Activated particles expand into the middle of their longest run of 3 to 5 empty neighbouring nodes
Particles that still have a neighbour are activated again
Final: no two particles are neighbours; none is activated, all stop

axes.name: Activation

values.label: adversarial activation
values.definition: The scheduler of the setting decides, fairly, when each particle is activated; an isolated particle may be activated, and a particle with a neighbour may wait any finite time.

values.label: event-driven activation (ED-Async)
values.definition: A contracted particle is activated as soon as it has, or gains, a neighbour, and a contracted particle with no neighbour is not activated. The adversary still chooses the duration of each activation, the time an expansion or a contraction takes, and the activation of expanded particles; operations stay non-atomic.

axes.origin: Navarra, Piselli and Prencipe introduced event-driven activation for scattering after showing that with a 1-hop view the problem is unsolvable when the adversary controls activations [Navarra2025Scattering]. Under it "the adversary does not control anymore the activation of contracted particles which becomes an event driven (ED) process"; they read it as sensing that reacts to the stimuli of neighbouring particles. In their words, "this kind of schedule, that we call ED-Async, is less general than the pure asynchronous one, but it is clearly more general than the synchronous case where all particles are always active" [Navarra2025Scattering]. It is kept as an axis of this problem rather than a value of the model's scheduler axis, because it neither implies nor follows from a sequential scheduler.
